title: The Second Arrow
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: The talk's main teaching emphasizes the importance of observing our experiences without judgment or attachment, allowing us to see things as they are rather than getting caught up in our conditioned thoughts and reactions. By recognizing this process, we can learn to let go of suffering caused by our reactivity and cultivate greater freedom and understanding. This involves developing mindfulness practices such as zazen and carefully considering teachings on faith, with the goal of creating a more authentic and peaceful way of living.

sentences.text: Good evening everybody.
I apologize on our behalf if you don't know that verse.
We were studying the other day about, we get concerned about these small details sometimes in religion, you know.
We had a whole meeting the other day about how to pass out and remember to pass out the little books with all the verses in them.
We have a plan and it just has yet to be implemented.

We have an action plan, so I won't even tell you what it is in case it changes, but hopefully soon we'll have a nice little plan and a book, a little book with the verse will just appear in your hands at the right time and I'll be clear what to do with it.
Or maybe not.
A few housekeeping announcements before tonight's dharma talk.
This dharma talk is a regular second Wednesday of the month talk, a formal talk which could be given by me or any other people who have done the right sort of trainings to give a formal dharma talk.
We have a few of them.
But starting next week we're going to jump out of our usual Wednesday night schedule, which has a sort of rotation of events, always starting with zazen and then something.
Starting next week we're going to jump out of that a little bit, and for six weeks have a seminar.
The seminar will look almost identical to tonight except we're calling it a seminar and it's a series.
It'll start with zazen.
I think it'll be a 40 minute period of zazen, and then probably not kinhin.
Then I want to lead us and facilitate for us a series of investigations into mindfulness, which is one core aspect of Buddhist teaching that's universal to all Buddhism.
Lately I've been studying a secular adaptation of, or not adaptation quite right, a secular expression of, implementation of it.
You are welcome to come to all six of those if you want to.
It'll be a series, so one will build on the next, but it's also fine to just come when you can, like always.
And if you prefer not to have this sort of noise and complication of all this seminar, you could also just come for zazen and then go on about your business for those six weeks.
If you're concerned about having enough zazen with the community, I also want to remind you that this is one meeting of four or five that we have each week.
So if your schedule allows you could also come Monday, Wednesday or Friday at noon, or Saturday morning, first and third Saturday mornings of the month.
There are three periods of zazen with the community.
And if you can't come to all of them and are interested, I'm going to do my level best to post materials on the website right away, so you can follow along.
A really core and important aspect of this seminar will be that it will be as experiential as possible.
It'll be about actual practices to do, some of which are quite familiar to us based in sitting meditation, some a little less so.

I'm going to try to create materials, mostly recordings, to support us in trying some of these practices at home, and if we pull it off, to try these practices at home in a fairly sustained and regular way.
We'll see what happens.
I think it will be fun.

In my experience with re-engaging in my own practice with mindfulness and trying some of these practices, some of which look sort of non-Zen and I would have probably sneered at some years ago, my experience has been that they're really helpful.
They're really shifting my sense of who this person is and how to practice, really changing my zazen, or my experience of zazen.
I don't know if zazen is exactly something that one changes, but my experience and understanding are shifting a little bit.
So anyway, if it sounds like a really crummy idea, I hope you'll be open minded and see if it turns out to be a crummy reality, because that's a very different thing from an idea.
Maybe it will be good.
The other thing that's interesting about the mind is that we hear something that maybe doesn't sound like a good idea and then we project that infinitely into the future.
This is just six weeks, and then we'll go back to the usual zazen.
So that's just a little footnote.
Tonight's talk, I want to bring up a short sutra from the Buddha, from the Pali Canon.
The Pali Canon is the oldest complete collection that's extant, that we still have, of what the Buddha may have taught.
One has to say "may have" because nothing was written down for some hundreds of years after the Buddha spoke.
That's worth thinking about for a minute.
Just think about all the things that have happened in our lives that may not have been written down.
We have some sense, maybe, of what happened 20 years ago or 30 years ago, depending on how old we are, 40 years ago, 50 years ago.
But who really knows what happened to them?
Do you really know?
The students of the Buddha made a really unbelievably energetic attempt to maintain some understanding, and even verbatim understanding, of what the Buddha taught.
But who really knows?
This is as close as we're going to get, so we might as well study them and see how they apply.

Of course one of the most famous teachings preserved through this mechanism of oral repetition, and one of the most famous sutras, which I'm not going to read tonight, but I'll read some other time, recommends that we not take any of this on faith, that we take it in respectfully and carefully and thoroughly and then see through our own experience, our own heart, whether it is true and helpful to us.
Sometimes in the religion business there's great concern about what's authentic and what's not authentic.
So these words of the Buddha, are they authentic or not?
I don't know.
"Lie on your backs and do a MBSR body scan next week," is that authentic or not?
I really don't know.
But we'll see whether it's helpful for us.
The central litmus test that the Buddha recommended, which we can't really argue with, is this.

In considering any teaching or decision or thought or word that we're going to say or thing we're going to do or vote we're going to cast, the core question is: did that lead to an increase in happiness and well-being for myself and others?
Did it?
Did things feel a little better in the world?
Or did that lead to a little more trouble, a little more confusion, a little more disconnect, a little more suffering?
Which is a different question from "is that authentic or not?"
Or "was I right?"
It's a different question even from was I right or not?
So let's consider this wonderful sutta.
I'm going to read it more or less straight through.
It's a couple of pages, with just a few comments (I'll try to restrain myself).
Then I want to give a few examples of how I've been noticing this lately, unfolding in my experience so far as I know it.
Then I'm going to invite us into pairs, or three people maybe, for a small group contemplation together: active listening, about how this seems to be unfolding for us and what we can do about it.
*So one time the Buddha said, monks, an uninstructed run-in-the-mill person feels feelings of pleasure, feelings of pain, feelings of neither pleasure nor pain.*
Okay, so that's the first thing.
Essentially somebody who's practicing has this range of experience.
Pleasant things happen, unpleasant things, neutral things happen.
And then he says:
*A well-instructed disciple of the noble ones also feels feelings of pleasure, feelings of pain, feelings of neither pleasure nor pain.*
So a practitioner, someone who's practicing the dharma, feels these things also.
What difference, what distinguishing factor is there between the well-instructed disciple of the noble ones and the uninstructed run-in-the-mill person?
*The monks answer, for us, Lord, the teachings of the blessed one has their root, their guide and their arbitrator.
It would be good if the blessed one would explicate the meaning of this statement.
Having heard it from the blessed ones, the monks will remember it.*
It seems to be a sort of fancy way of saying we have no idea: please tell us.
And the Buddha says:
*In that case, monks, listen and pay close attention.
I will speak.*
*As you say, teacher, the monks responded.
So the blessed one said, when touched with a feeling of pain, the uninstructed run-in-the-mill person sorrows, grieves and laments, beats her breast, becomes distraught.
And so he feels two pains, physical and mental.*
So we're starting with the example of the physical pain.
*Just as if they were to shoot a man with an arrow, and right afterwards were to shoot her or him with another arrow, so that she would feel the pain of two arrows.
In the same way, when touched with a feeling of pain, the uninstructed run-in-the-mill person sorrows, grieves and laments, beats his breast, and becomes distraught.
So he feels two pains, mental and physical.
As he is touched by that painful feeling, he is resistant.
Any resistance, obsession with regard to that painful feeling, obsesses him or her.
And touched by this painful feeling, she then delights in sensual pleasure.*
It's a little bit confusing.
We'll unpack this, but right away you get the sense of an analysis of a lot of stuff that goes on, an inquiry into what goes on when there's an unpleasant sensation.
Lots of stuff.
And we know that.
*Why is this?
Because the uninstructed run-in-the-mill person does not discern any escape from painful feeling aside from sensual pleasure.
He does not discern any escape from painful feeling aside from sensual pleasure.
As she is always delighting in sensual pleasure, any passion, obsession with regard to that feeling of pleasure, obsesses her.
He does not discern, as it actually is present, the origination, passing away, allure, drawback, or escape from that feeling.

And as she does not discern the origination, passing away, allure, drawback, or escape from that feeling, then any ignorance, obsession with regard to that feeling of neither pleasure nor pain, obsesses him.*
Does that make any sense?
So that was a whole analysis of pain.
Now there's going to be an analysis of pleasure.
*Sensing a feeling of pleasure, she senses it as though joined with it.
As though joined with it.
Sensing a feeling of pain, he senses it as though joined with it.
Sensing a feeling of neither pleasure nor pain, she senses that as though joined with it.
This is called an uninstructed run-in-the-mill person.
Joined with birth, aging, and death, sorrows, lamentations, and pain, distress, and despair.
She is joined, I tell you, with birth, suffering, and stress.*
I prefaced that not quite right.
First there was an analysis of the process, and then there was an analysis of not distinguishing that the whole process is going on.
So being lost in this and not knowing that it's happening: identifying.
Now we're going to contrast with you excellent practitioners who don't have this problem.
*Now, the well-instructed disciple of the noble ones, when touched with a feeling of pain, does not sorrow, grieve, or lament.
Does not beat her breasts or become distraught.
And so he feels just one pain.
Physical but not mental.
Just as if they were to shoot a man with an arrow and right afterwards not shoot him with another arrow, so that she would feel the pain of only one arrow.*
There's a wonderful logic and consistency in these arguments.
*In the same way, when touched with a feeling of pain, the well-instructed disciple of the noble one does not sorrow, grieve, or lament.
Does not beat her breasts or become distraught.
She just feels one pain.
Physical, not mental.*
Then we'll unpack the rest of this process.
*As she is touched by the painful feeling, she is not resistant.
No resistance, obsession with regard to that painful feeling obsesses her.
Touched by that painful feeling, she does not delight in sensual pleasure.
Why is that?
Because the well-instructed disciple of the noble ones discerns an escape from painful feeling aside from sensual pleasure.
As he is not delighting in sensual pleasure, no passion, obsession with regard to that feeling of pleasure obsesses her.
He discerns as it actually is present the origination, passing away, allure, drawback, and escape from that feeling.
As he discerns this origination, passing away, allure, drawback, and escape, no ignorance, obsession with regard to that feeling obsesses him or her.*
So that's some sequence of events around sensations.
*And then, sensing a feeling of pleasure, he senses it disjoined from it.*
There are a couple of different ways of translating this, and "disjoined" is awkward.
This is a very literal translator.
There's a different way it's translated, and I'm not remembering what word is used, but "disjoined" is awkward.
So: not lost in it.
Some sense of freedom and space.
*Sensing a feeling of pleasure, he senses it disjoined from it.
Sensing a feeling of pain, he senses it disjoined from it.
Sensing a feeling of neither pleasure nor pain, he senses it disjoined from it.
This is called a well-instructed disciple of the noble ones disjoined from the birth, aging, and death, sorrows, lamentations, pains, distresses, and despairs.
He is disjoined,*
I tell you, from suffering and stress.
So this is the difference.
This is the distinction.
This is the distinguishing factor between the well-instructed disciple of the noble ones and the uninstructed run-of-the-mill person.
So this is the difference.
This is the distinction.
This is the distinction factor between the well-instructed disciple of the noble ones and the uninstructed run-of-the-mill person.
And that's the end of the sutta.
So it's pretty short, but very dense.
And the Buddha and his disciples also developed a fair amount of language just to try to describe all this.
And they were starting with language.
They were speaking in a sort of early dialect of Sanskrit, and later it got translated into Pali, which is kind of the high Latin of Buddhism.
And even the language they were starting with, I think, had more words for these inner processes than we have in English.
And then it further gets translated into English, so it's a little awkward.
So a little bit of background and unpacking is always needed.
But the basic idea is pretty simple, and I think we can relate to it if we think about it.
And that is reactivity.
And that the basis of reactivity is some misunderstanding of reality, of the way things actually are.
And what's implied here, the basis of that misunderstanding, is our strong belief in a separate, sort of fragile self that has to be protected.
So there's always some sense of self-protection in that reactivity.
Life is inevitably not without pain, not without difficulty.
Things don't go the way one would like.
There are troubles.
But that we add to that.
And what we add to that is so quickly added, as he says in here, these experiences we sense as if joined to them.
So our reactivity and our sort of additional psychophysical narrative that's added to each positive or negative experience is added so quickly and so thoroughly.
What he's teaching here is the uninstructed person is not able to distinguish this sort of foundational experience from the elaboration.
And so therefore it's as if something bad happens to you and you immediately knock yourself in the head.
Like, so fast.
You think, "God, why did he hit me?"
And so fast.
Because of a lack of understanding of this process.
And I'm kind of working my way backwards here a little bit.
So that's one point.
He's saying there's a lack of understanding that there's a process that's happening, because of being too sort of immersed and caught within this process as if this process were you.

And then the next thing he's saying, rolling it back, is not being able to discern accurately that every sort of iota, or every sort of atom of experience, to use, if we can use science language, has a sort of trajectory of its own.
And this is a lot of what we're studying in meditation.

If you quiet the mind, you start to see that what seems at first to be a sort of very dense, solid, continuous narrative, you know, me, me, me, me, me, me, me, me, me, me, basically, right, is actually made up of many individual, apparently sort of individual events that appear and disappear, right, arise and fall.
And as we practice and sort of settle into the breath and the body, sometimes on a good day we can distinguish, "Oh, a judgmental thought just arose and it passed away again.
That's just breath."
Oh, you know, a sound was just cognized, you know.
Was there somebody like swearing just outside the window a little while ago?
Was that just like, like that, like, oh, and then passed away again.
That was a good example, because whoever that was then never said another word or left or something.
Was that person even there?
We don't know.
Right?
We don't know.

And so this is a sort of understanding that's absolutely supported by practice, absolutely supported by the practice of quieting the mind, starting to watch things come and go and starting to be a little less sure of, you know, "I am this person constantly buffeted and beat up by all these other people running around swearing outside windows and, you know, judging me and, you know, myself judging myself," and all this.
So he's saying awareness of that arising and falling.
And he describes a whole sort of technical sequence, which I won't get into, which is translated here as origination, passing away.
And you think that would be the end of it, right?
So he said origination, passing away.
And there's a whole bunch more things that happen.
The Buddha taught, which are here translated as allure, drawback and escape.
So I'll just leave that hanging out there for future study.
That there's some, in a way, sort of [unclear: "Dharma's work"], there seems to be some sort of residue, even after it passes away, different aspects of that passing away.

So this is before, so before we even get to any sort of trying to think about our thinking or think about what happens to us, the Buddha is suggesting there's some sort of very quiet, low-level processes to investigate.
The first being not being so sort of caught in this as if it were really real.
The second being starting to actually sort of cognize more accurately.
Arising and passing away, arising and passing away.
And what we think of as a sort of continuity of our life is just a sort of complicated sort of interweaving of all these things arising and passing away all the time.
Okay?
And then, backing it up a little bit further, he talks about what is the sort of flavor.
Nancy gave a wonderful talk a few months ago or something about the [unclear: "flavor over life"].
He says, what is the sort of habitual flavor that arises in response to a painful thing?
And what he suggests is there's somebody who's a non-practitioner, and he's using sort of extremes on purpose here, right?
It's understood that even the monks had all these problems, right?
That's understood.
There's no pure monks who are perfect and uninstructed worldlings who are just a disaster, right?
Everyone has some combination of these things going on all the time.
So what he's saying, with the extreme example of the uninstructed run-of-the-mill.
Usually this is "uninstructed worldling," which sounds sort of quaint, but here he uses "run-of-the-mill person."
But the way they respond to pain is in two ways.
First is resistance.
I don't want that.
I don't deserve that.
It's not my fault.
I don't want to get away.
And the second is reaching for pleasure as an alternative to that.
So if we can't shove it away, we could pour in a lot of pleasure to dilute it.
And such a person does not see any alternative because of action.
So that's the lack of freedom, right?
That's the lack of freedom.
Something bad happens to me.
I only have one thing I can do.
It doesn't work.
I try something else.
That doesn't work either.
And I'm really upset.
I just got shot by two arrows.
And then I'm going to stumble on and hope I don't get shot again.
Maybe I just dodge a lot or something.
And he's saying, in contrast, our perfect practitioner, which is also us, does not resist.
Recognizes that experience is just experience.
What happens just happens.
Some sensation arising from the feeling of the skin, from the eyes, from the ears, from the nose, from the mind, is just experience.
And there's no need to resist it or try to get rid of it or fix it.
And there's also nothing to be gained from trying to pour in pleasure as an alternative.
That simply won't work.
Won't help.
So that's the next set of contrasts.
And the last set of contrasts is in a way just another take on that.
I meant to go back to another translation, but I didn't have time.
This translation starts with physical pain.
And usually what they do is they repeat this formula with all the five classical aggregates of reality, which essentially function the same way.
So I want to mention those just briefly.
The first is our physicality.
The first aspect of our being is matter.
So the first kind of pain that one could think about is somebody pokes you.
You stub your toe or somebody hits you in a bar fight or something.
Some physical thing happens.
Or some internal pain.
You have a pain in your stomach.
Pain from illness or pain from aging.
But then one could also have pain in other dimensions of our living.
It doesn't have to be actual physical sensation.
It could be pain from having any quality of experience that's not pleasant.
A mental experience that's in some way not pleasant.
Not what we like.
It could be from having, which is feeling, the second of these aggregates.
It could be from having some impulse that we don't like.
Like wanting, whatever it is for us.
Some impulse to be aggressive.
Some impulse to drink.
Some impulse to do something that we know is unskillful and harmful.
That's a certain kind of pain, right?
It could be a pain from having a thought arise that we don't like.
That's a certain kind of pain.
And we don't always recognize that as a pain because we self-identify with that.
We think, oh, it's me, I'm such a schmuck or something.
But that's the secondary process that he's talking about.
So there's a pain from mental formations in the mind.
And there's a certain kind of pain just from the nature of consciousness that happens, that we also run this whole tape on.
So he's using physical pain as an example of a much broader mental, emotional, physical, spiritual apparatus.
What he's saying is that very quickly, in the very same domain that it happens, the uninstructed person, the non-practitioner, manages to generate a secondary pain.
And you can see this happening, right?
Somebody pokes you and right away the body clenches, right?
The body tightens.
There's a secondary pain.
And then the whole thing unfolds.
Why'd you do that?
I never wanted you for a brother anyway.
And on and on it goes.
So I can attempt a class to unpack a lot of the Buddhist psychology in here, but I didn't really do that for tonight.
We probably don't want me to do that anyway, just time-wise.
But that's the basic idea.

To study this process, and he's suggesting, he's saying, look and see: an almost instantaneous second pain generated through habit in that same domain, and then the cascading process, running through the whole mind-body cycle of resistance, seeking pleasure, and being immersed in the whole process with identity, as if it was you.
As if it was you.
On the one hand.
On the other hand, not creating that secondary pain within that domain, not running that whole process of resistance and seeking pleasurable alternatives.
And all this runs the other direction, too.
There's a certain kind of suffering from pleasure.
There's a certain kind of suffering in pleasure itself, where all this stuff works, and you just reverse the words.
There's a kind of seeking for a painful phenomenon when there's pleasure, too.
That sounds really creepy, right, but it's true.
Check it out.

So, not doing all that, and then I forgot the other point, and seeing a moment-by-moment unfolding, arising and falling of phenomena as just arising and falling of phenomena, and not being caught in that, and immersed in that, as if it was you.
And then he has a little poem for us.
So we'll read you his little poem, and I'll mention just a few times lately that I've been noticing something along these lines in my life.
And we can see what you think of, or what occurs to you.
Because all of this is just interesting, or maybe a little boring, if it's not about you, if it's not about your actual life.
So here's a little poem, which just restates what he already said.
*The discerning person, learned, doesn't sense a feeling of pleasure or pain.
This is the difference in skillfulness between the sage and the person run of the mill.
For a learned person who has fathomed the Dharma, clearly seeing this world in the next, desirable things don't charm the mind.
Undesirable things bring no resistance.
His acceptance and rejection are scattered, gone to their end, do not exist.
Knowing the dustless, sorrowless state he discerns rightly, has gone beyond becoming, to the further shore.*
I apologize for all the male pronouns everywhere.
It's just what we end up with.
I'm not going to try to change around in a poem.
So one more time on that.
*The discerning person, learned, doesn't sense a feeling of pleasure or pain.* Doesn't categorize things maybe so rigidly.
*This is the difference in skillfulness between the sage and the person run of the mill.
For a learned person who has fathomed the Dharma, clearly seeing this world in the next, desirable things don't charm the mind.
Undesirable things bring no resistance.
His acceptance and rejection are scattered, gone to their end,*
*do not exist.
Knowing the dustless, sorrowless state he discerns rightly, has gone beyond becoming, to the further shore.*

That one line that was interesting was about his acceptance and rejection: *"His acceptance and rejection are scattered, gone to their end, do not exist."* So in other words, not clinging to rejection and acceptance itself either.
He's not saying, "Here's a great new idea: accept everything.
That's actually who you are."
Not that either.
Acceptance and rejection are just scattered, scattered to the waves.
So here are a few things I've noticed lately in this arena, which is the arena of our whole life.
The first thing I noticed lately was a quite strong experience of, I suppose you might call it, role stress.
An important part of our construct of self is that we have certain roles, right?
At first, as we're growing up, I think we think we just have one role.
That's part of the stress of adolescence, I think: we realize that actually I have multiple roles in life, and in different roles I'm kind of a different person.
But I have my roles.
Some roles I feel comfortable in, some not so comfortable, but these are the roles that constellate me.
I am a daughter or a son or a father or this kind of worker or that kind of professional or this kind of person or somebody who's into this but not into that.
So we have these self-definitional roles.
When we put ourselves in a situation in which those roles don't seem to quite apply, it can be stressful and confusing.
For many of us who are attracted to Dharma, it's like going to a big party.
It can be this way.
I don't have a very well-defined party person role, and so I find parties pretty stressful.
How long should I talk to this person?
How long should I stand here?
What should I talk about?
Should I drink this?
So there's this stress from roles, which points to the underlying fragility and unreliability of roles as a way to take care of ourselves.
But they arise out of experience and we have them.
Or they have us.
I went last week, I was in Massachusetts and New York, and in Massachusetts I went to a scientific conference.
I was there for a reason.
I didn't just randomly go to a scientific conference where I'd have no role at all.
I went to an ophthalmology conference or something.
I went to a scientific conference on mindfulness.

So science is starting to get interesting, well, some small subsection of science, but actual real scientists, real people with PhDs and labs and everything, are doing studies on the effects of meditation.
There have been studies for a while, including studies on this self-reported "I feel better because of meditation, I feel better in these ways."
But now they also have new, and some of them really quite new, ways of actually watching the brains of people.
They're doing these studies, and lo and behold, it turns out meditation actually changes your brain.
There's a small but scientifically quite valid body of evidence around this.

So I was going to this conference where they were presenting new studies and showing PowerPoint slides and talking about statistical analysis and having more or less polite arguments about the validity of different ways of going about things.
People were wearing button-down shirts and name tags, and it was a fancy conference hotel and all this.

I found myself very uncomfortable, very uncomfortable, and a persistent thought kept arising, something along the lines of: I don't belong here, I never went to graduate school, I don't work in a lab, I don't have a university affiliation, I don't work for an institution, I'm going to be found out.
I did actually wear one of my button-down shirts, so I was trying to blend in.
But I had spent quite a bit of time thinking about whether to have my mala beads on my wrist or not.
It was surprising how much the mind was taken up with these kinds of thoughts, despite all evidence to the contrary.
I would meet somebody at one of the meals.
People were pretty friendly, actually.
You sit down next to somebody before the thing starts and they say, "Oh, hi, how are you?
I'm from such and such.
Why are you here?"
"Oh, okay."
I would introduce myself as a teacher interested in mindfulness, and 100% of the time they were quite friendly and happy to meet me and thought that was really wonderful.
They were interested, wanted to hear about the center and wanted to talk about it, and [unclear: "won my card"].
So I was quite warmly received, but I had this strongly persistent stress about roles and feeling like I didn't belong there.
I was pretty upset a good amount of the time by this, and distracted by it, which made it difficult to actually attend.
I wasn't totally crawling up the walls, but I was a little bit agitated by this.
Then I was trying to study this and notice this.
What I was noticing, and this is interesting, was that the first arrow was not physical.
Nobody poked me.
It was not vision.
Nobody even looked at me funny, as far as I know.
It was not hearing.
Nobody said to me, "Why are you here?
Can I see your CV?"
It was not any of those things.
The actual first arrow was a conditioned thought.
It was a conditioned thought: I don't belong here.
Then the second arrow was additional thoughts, supporting that and reinforcing that and looking for evidence of that.
Even though I didn't find evidence of that, still looking for evidence of that.
Maybe that guy over there doesn't like me.
Then what I noticed was this seeking for an escape.
In my case it seemed to be that I was alone, without my usual support structure of my family life and coming to the Zendo and all this.
So I noticed that my conduct in terms of taking care of myself at the hotel was really crummy.
I was staying up late watching TV.
I was not eating very well.
And therefore, because I was staying up late, I was not sleeping very well.
That was helping to create conditions where this could continue to happen.
And so I was like that through this whole meeting.
And so it goes.
How should I study this?
How should I work with this?
Is it a matter of just going to enough of these meetings that I create a new role?
Like, okay, now I have a role of Tim, Zen teacher, student of mindfulness at a meeting on mindfulness.
Tada!
Here I am!
I'm very self-assured now.
I'm in my role.
